articles.title: Brisbane 2032 Olympics: The Fitzroy River in Queensland, Australia has 500 crocodiles in it - but that's not the main concern
articles.summary: Queensland's Fitzroy River has been selected for the 2032 Games, despite concerns over the course - and its inhabitants.
articles.body:
The annual rowing regatta for schools in the Australian state of Queensland usually passes off without too much attention.

Each year more than 600 of the state's most promising teenage rowers battle it out on the crocodile-inhabited Fitzroy River, in the city of Rockhampton.

"We've never had any media wanting to attend here," Anthea O'Loughlin, head of Rowing Queensland, tells the BBC.

But this year is different. In six years' time, the 2032 Brisbane Olympics and Paralympics are set to stage rowing and canoe sprint events in this very stretch of water, which has just passed a technical assessment and been endorsed as safe and fair for athletes.

While sightings of saltwater crocodiles on the river – which number around 500 and can grow to four metres (13ft) long – are not uncommon, state government files going back more than 40 years record no attacks by the reptiles on humans.

And while influential figures at last month's World Rowing congress in Amsterdam made occasional references to "safety", the presence of the reptiles was not their chief concern.

"Fairness" is what's been raised with British Rowing's chief executive Tom Solesbury – a reference to the tidal river's natural bends and currents, which many in the rowing community say make it unsuitable for elite competition.

Drew Ginn, who has won three Olympic gold medals for Australia in rowing, told BBC Radio he had concerns over potential flooding and "fairness and integrity" at the venue.

"Personally, I'm not fearful of the Australian animals but I've never had a crocodile near me," he said.

"I'm sure I'd row faster, I'm sure all the athletes would row faster. That's on the list of concerns, I don't think it's the highest priority in concerns but it was certainly cited very early on."

The German rowing body's president Moritz Petri said athletes had also questioned the sustainability of holding the event some 600km (373 miles) from Brisbane.

But the "so-called impediments" got short shrift from the most senior politician in Queensland, state premier David Crisafulli, who reached for less diplomatic language.

"Let's be honest, let's scratch beneath the surface and call it for what it is," he said days after the Amsterdam meeting.

"It is a group of interstate and overseas elites who are trying to bully their way because they don't want to go to regional Queensland and that's not right."

Rowing chiefs contacted by the BBC before Thursday's decision declined to comment directly on Crisafulli's "elites" remarks.

But both Petri and Simon Wickham, chief executive of Rowing New Zealand, said their concerns had nothing to do with regional or urban preference but with competitors getting fair racing.

Petri added it was about what's best for their athletes who will train four years for the event, "dreaming night [after] night of becoming an Olympic champion".

Whether it was crocs or currents that tipped the balance, ultimately it was the sport's governing body World Rowing and the International Olympic Committee (IOC) that had the final say on the river's suitability.

On Thursday they approved it after a technical assessment by an engineering firm and the Games' infrastructure authority – which looked at the riverbed, competition course, river flows, water levels and likely weather conditions during the Games.

"Based on the extensive analysis undertaken, we now know that the Fitzroy River is capable of providing fair competition conditions during the period of the Games," World Rowing president Jean-Christophe Rolland said.

There was also now "confidence" in the river for canoe sprint athletes, said Thomas Konietzko, president of that sport's governing body, Paddle Worldwide.

The state premier was delighted. "The Fitzroy has passed with flying colours," an upbeat Crisafulli told parliament. "It's official. Signed, sealed and delivered."

In backing Rockhampton, the state government ignored a 2025 report it commissioned itself, which found the location unsuitable and concluded the best option would be to use a course built in Sydney for the 2000 Olympics.

The Fitzroy now needs to pass a final assessment of its design, value for money and long-term community legacy. As the decision rests with the state government, it's unlikely to fall at this hurdle.

But a wider debate will continue over whether Rockhampton is the right place to invest heavily in rowing facilities – and whether it can accommodate the 2032 influx of visitors.

The city is surrounded by cattle producers and normally experiences its peak number of guests every three years during Beef Week.

They're not mentioned anywhere in the latest update from the IOC and World Rowing and they weren't considered in the technical assessment.

The safety management plan for this weekend's school regatta does however mention the word "crocodile" 28 times.

"The Fitzroy River is within recognised crocodile country," it says.

"Event planning must therefore assume that a crocodile sighting is possible… No natural waterway in crocodile country can be guaranteed to be crocodile-free."

Procedures this weekend include suspending racing and competitors returning to the bank if a croc is spotted. The official signal for a sighting is the call of "crocodile, crocodile, crocodile".

Asked specifically about crocodiles, New Zealand's Wickham told the BBC the primary concern was ensuring the "fairest possible course" for rowers. "We would obviously expect any course chosen to be safe for rowers," he added.

The company owned by Australia's richest person Gina Rinehart, Hancock Prospecting, which supported Rockhampton's bid and has pumped millions into sports including rowing, pointed to "fake media" concerns about risks posed by flooding and crocodiles in the Fitzroy.

"The people of Rocky for many years have sent their own children to train in this river, and for competitions, without a single crocodile incident," a spokesperson said in a statement.

Brisbane 2032's chief executive has said organisers are making contingency plans "as we would for any venue".

The 2000 Olympics venue in Sydney is ready and waiting as a backup – though that would be unconscionable for Queenslanders.

For the school-age rowers at this weekend's regatta, none of this debate really matters as they take to the water.

Among them are potentially some contenders for the 2032 Games.

"For our students, the Fitzroy is first and foremost their home water," says Phillip Moulds, headmaster of The Rockhampton Grammar School.

"The Fitzroy has also been the starting point for many… some of whom have gone on to compete at the highest levels of the sport nationally and internationally."

articles.title: 'No going home till I win': Mirabai Chanu’s Asian Games mission to end India’s 28-year wait
articles.summary: Asian Games 2026 News: Ever wondered what it feels like to lift nearly double your body weight over your head? That is exactly what two-time Olympic medallist Mirabai Chanu .
articles.body: Ever wondered what it feels like to lift nearly double your body weight over your head? That is exactly what two-time Olympic medallist Mirabai Chanu has been doing for more than a decade.And in about a week’s time, she will again attempt to do exactly that when she competes in women’s 49kg category in Aichi-Nagoya, hoping to win the one pice of glory that still eludes her glittering career — an Asian Games medal.Determined to finally break the jinx, Mirabai has left nothing to chance in her preparations. From returning to training within days of winning her third consecutive Commonwealth Games gold medal to regularly consulting American strength and conditioning coach Dr Aaron Horschig, she has been meticulous in her pursuit of success.The Asian Games has been the one major event where circumstances and injuries have repeatedly stood in her way.The 32-year-old first competed at the continental showpiece as a teenager in Incheon in 2014, finishing ninth. A back injury forced her to miss the 2018 edition in Jakarta, while hip and thigh injuries hampered her campaign in Hangzhou three years ago, where she narrowly missed the podium and finished fourth.This time, she heads to Japan on the back of a dominant showing in Glasgow, where she won her third successive CWG gold. Competing in the women’s 48kg category, Mirabai registered a Games-record total of 190kg, a staggering 22kg more than runner-up Ruth Asuquo Nyong.The triumph added to an already remarkable collection that includes an Olympic silver medal, a world championship title and multiple CWG podium finishes.Yet her focus has now shifted to the title that has evaded her accomplishments.Speaking to SAI Media after coming back from Glasgow, she said: “I was straight back to training at Modinagar. articles.title: How the women's 800m became athletics' headline act
articles.summary: After making its debut at the 1928 Olympics, the women's 800m was cut from the programme. Now, it's often billed as the must-see event of major athletics championships. So, how did we get here?
articles.body:
For 32 years, the women's 800m was absent from the Olympics, with its competitors deemed too frail. Now, it is one of the most hotly anticipated events on the track.

This extraordinary story starts at the 1928 Olympic Games, which represented a huge - if temporary - step forward for women's sports.

The Amsterdam Games were the first to allow women to compete in track and field events. Five women's events were added to the programme - the 100m, high jump, discus, 400m hurdles and, controversially at the time, 800m.

German athlete Karoline Lina Radke , external became the first woman to win Olympic gold in the 800m - but she would also be the last for another 32 years.

The event was removed from the Games after reports - later proven to be false - claimed competitors suffered extreme exhaustion after the race, and the International Olympic Committee decided women were too frail to compete , external over the two-lap distance.

Fast forward almost 100 years and the event now gets headline status at major events.

In recent times, it's been the battle between Britain's Olympic 800m champion Keely Hodgkinson and the Swiss European champion Audrey Werro that has captivated fans.

So how did the 800m become the 'one to watch'? BBC Sport spoke to the women who helped shape the race to find out.

It was the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, and Ann Brightwell (nee Packer) had just crossed the finish line of the women's 800m to take gold - and set a new world record.

In doing so, Brightwell became the first British woman to win an Olympic gold on the track, in a time of two minutes 01.1 seconds.

She told BBC Sport: "My husband, who was my fiance then, said to me, 'you don't realise what you've done'.

"I didn't give it a thought at the time… but now I realise I played a very small part in women running longer distances."

But the controversy hadn't completely gone away. Brightwell knew all about the claims that had seen women unable to compete for 32 years after the 800m was removed from the Olympics.

Brightwell adds: "Men weren't happy about women competing in these very high profile events…we were considered too frail and too delicate.

"And they took it upon themselves to make it look really bad. They were saying women were collapsing on the way round. But it was all a lie."

After 1928, women's middle-distance shrunk into the shadows for the next few decades.

The 800m was finally reintroduced to the Olympic programme in 1960 and, four years later, the then-22-year-old Brightwell went to her first Olympics, fitting training around her job as a teacher.

"Many people in my era either had to take unpaid leave or resign, or they got sacked because they were trying to juggle their sports with their career," she said.

"My school was very tolerant towards what I was doing, so I was fortunate."

Going out for a run around the local streets or countryside - which seems so commonplace today - was unusual in the era Brightwell was competing.

"If I just felt like an easy run, I would run around my village, around the streets… people commented on it or tooted their horns. And it was funny looking back, but it never troubled me," the now 84-year-old told BBC Sport.

Brightwell's 800m time of 2:01.1 stood for almost three years, before Australian Judy Pollock broke that with a new time of 2:01 flat in 1967.

The next target was to go under two minutes.

Breaking 'sub-two' - and a stubborn world record

"Records are great and medals are the best, but when you break a barrier it's a fantastic feeling," said Christina Boxer-Cahill (nee Boxer).

It was at the 1979 European Cup final in Turin that Boxer-Cahill looked up at the clock and realised she'd gone under two minutes.

She added: "I knew this would probably be my last chance, because there were other girls in Britain trying to do it."

In 1971, Germany's Hildegard Falck , external had become the first woman to break the two-minute barrier.

Eight years later, it was the 22-year-old Boxer-Cahill who became the first British woman to do so, in a time of one minute 59.05 seconds.

"It's a bit like when Roger Bannister broke four minutes for the mile. Once he'd done it everybody did it because you see what's possible," Boxer-Cahill, who is now 69 years old, told BBC Sport.

"I just think I'm so fortunate that I was in a sport where everybody accepted that you have men and women's races in the Olympics."

From 1971 to 1983, the women's 800m world record would be broken six times.

It belongs to Czech athlete Jarmila Kratochvilova, who ran a time of one minute 53.28 seconds at a meeting in Munich.

Kratochvilova's record has been questioned, with claims it was assisted by her country's doping regime that existed at the time, something she has strenuously denied.

In 2017, European Athletics proposed wiping out records set before 2005 - sending a strong signal that records set before then were disputable.

Several Soviet satellite states - including East Germany - are known to have been operating state-sponsored doping programmes throughout the 1980s.

At the 1988 Seoul Olympics, Boxer-Cahill finished fourth in the 1500m, behind a Russian athlete who was later banned for doping.

Boxer-Cahill said: "I was running during that Eastern Bloc era when, you know, they've looked back and some of the performances, there's sort of a cloud over it.

"I'd just have loved to have been on that rostrum. I wish the Eastern Bloc system hadn't been there, but that's what it was.

"Politics in sport, when you're the performer, it frustrates you. But if you get too frustrated, all it's going to do is upset your own performance."

"We've got not just two but several girls who are running under two minutes every time they turn out," Brightwell told BBC Sport.

Kratochvilova's 43-year-old record is looking increasingly precarious.

The 800m European champion Werro has come closest, running a time just 0.42 seconds shy of the record at the Zurich Diamond League.

Keely Hodgkinson, the current 800m indoor world record holder, told BBC Sport earlier this year that she's never felt closer to breaking the outdoor record.

She said: "I really do believe we can break it, but a lot of things have got to come together."

Hodgkinson is one of six athletes competing in the 800m at Athlos, the all-female athletics event taking place in London, on Friday.

"I do think the [800m] world record will go in the next year or two, and hopefully this season, because we're on a real high, aren't we?" Boxer-Cahill told BBC Sport.

"If it happens towards the end of the season, 2026 [would be] the year of women's 800m running."

articles.title: Officials defend using temporary containers, cruise ship as lodging at Asian Games
articles.summary: The Olympic Council of Asia is attempting to quell complaints about lodging for athletes and officials at the Asian Games, which includes the use of converte...
articles.body:
NAGOYA, Japan (AP) — The Olympic Council of Asia is attempting to quell complaints about lodging for athletes and officials at the Asian Games , which includes the use of converted wooden containers.

The OCA said Friday that all "17,000-plus athletes and officials" that registered by the entry deadline in July have been provided "games-appropriate accommodation."

The games open officially on Saturday and run through Oct. 4 in and around the central city of Nagoya, and feature at least 11,000 athletes, more than the Summer Olympics. They showcase 43 sports and 45 countries and regions.

Japanese officials decided against building a dedicated athletes villages and opted for accommodations on a cruise ship , in hotel rooms and in temporary wood containers.

Several countries have complained openly about the lodging, some basketball players have said the beds are too short, and hundreds of athletes had to be evacuated last week after heavy rainfall in the region.

"We don't want to leave a white elephant after the games here," Tayyab Ikram, deputy chairman of the Olympic Council of Asia athletes commission, said Friday at a news conference. "So it was not easy discussions, but it was also not a compromise, because then we find a very unique kind of alternatives."

Cost saving is a major issue in Japan, which spent an estimated $13 billion to organize the 2020 Tokyo Olympics , which were delayed a year by the pandemic. A government audit office suggested the real costs were probably twice that high.

The Italian cruise ship "Costa Serena" is docked at a port in Nagoya and will lodge up to 5,000 athletes and officials. Many athletes will be rotated in and out as events end and new events begin.

Cruise ships have been used before a large international sports events.

Part of the problem seemed to arise after the July deadline when late entries surfaced. In addition, new sports like Teqball, mixed martial arts and padel were added.

"It's very easy, you can insist on the athletes village," said Husain Al Musallam, the director general of the Olympic Council of Asia. "And then you build the athletes village, you spend such amount of money, and then we need to see what's going to happen after the games."

SNTV video journalist Raj Mohan contributed to this story.

articles.title: Ingebrigtsen se mide a Gressier y la armada africana, en los Mundiales de ruta
articles.standfirst: Se disputan las pruebas de la milla, los 5 kilómetros y medio maratón
articles.summary: Se disputan las pruebas de la milla, los 5 kilómetros y medio maratón
articles.body: Los Mundiales de ruta, que se disputan en Copenhague (Dinamarca) este fin de semana, reúnen a una gran nómina de las estrellas del mediofondo, entre ellos el noruego Jakob Ingebrigtsen y el francés Jimmy Gressier, que buscarán su cuota de protagonismo en los 5 kilómetros junto con el estadounidense Yared Nuguse en la milla ante la condición de favorita de la armada africana en el medio maratón. Tras el éxito de la primera edición en Riga (Letonia) en 2023, Copenhague acoge este campeonato para concluir la temporada oficial de eventos organizados por World Athletics. La prueba femenina de la milla reúne a buena parte de las mejores mediofondistas africanas, como la etíope Freyweni Hailu, que buscará mejorar su segundo puesto de Riga en 2023. Desde entonces, se ha convertido dos veces en campeona mundial en pista cubierta, terminó sexta en los 1.500 metros en el Mundial de Tokio de 2025 y ganó recientemente los 5.000 de la última final de la Liga Diamante. La francesa Agathe Guillemot, sexta en la final de la Liga Diamante, estuvo entre sus rivales en los 1.500 metros en el Ultimate de Budapest, en el que también compitieron la estadounidense Addison Wiley, medallista de bronce mundial en pista cubierta en los 800 metros en Torun en marzo, y la australiana Sarah Billings, bronce en los 800 metros de los Juegos de la Commonwealth En la categoría masculina de la milla las miradas están puestas en el estadounidense Yared Nuguse, que hará un cambio de pista a ruta seis días después de haber finalizado quinto en los 1.500 metros en el Ultimate de Budapest. El medallista de bronce olímpico en 1500 metros y antiguo poseedor del récord mundial de la milla en pista cubierta ya ha demostrado su habilidad en ruta, al ganar el título estadounidense en abril con un tiempo de 3:54.06. Su compatriota Vicent Ciattei se perfila como seria amenaza a juzgar por su rendimiento en la distancia. Además de terminar a poco más de medio segundo de Nuguse en el Campeonato de Estados Unidos, ha tenido un año excepcional en la pista, rebajando su mejor marca en los 1.500 metros a 3:30.90 y su mejor marca en la milla a 3:48.34. En esa terna de aspirantes a ganar también figuran el alemán Robert Farken, el galés Jake Heyward y el irlandés Andrew Coscoran El equipo español estará formado por cuatro atletas. Said Mechaal, que tiene 1.00.26 acreditada como marca personal en la distancia, y Marta Galimany, con 1:09:22, disputarán el medio maratón. A ellos se suman en las distancias más cortas Marta García, en los 5 kilómetros, y Martín Segurola, en la milla. Tras una victoria aplastante en el Ultimate de Budapest, la etíope Likina Amebaw intentará añadir otro título mundial a su palmarés en los 5 kilómetros ruta de Copenhague, a los que llega como número uno del 'ranking' mundial. Sus logros en ruta son igualmente impresionantes con 29:29 en los 10 km en Valencia en enero y una mejor marca personal de 14:23 en los 5 kilómetros, establecida en Barcelona a finales del año pasado. Amebaw no tendrá mucho respiro en el rápido circuito de Copenhague, sobre todo por parte de Aleshign Baweke, su compañera de equipo etíope, que buscará sorprender con una victoria que también quieren las kenianas Caroline Nyaga, que posee la mejor marca personal en 5 kilómetros entre las participantes de Copenhague con 14:19; y Caroline Gitonga, que ha protagonizado una de las temporadas más destacadas en carreras de ruta con 14:26 en 5 km. Europa también cuenta con varias atletas que aspiran a medalla como la neerlandesa Diane van Es, plusmarquista continental desde el pasado febrero con 14:33; y la belga Jana Van Lent, que en enero rebajó su récord nacional de 10 kilómetros en ruta a 30:10, estableció otro récord nacional de 14:36 en 5 kilómetros en Utrecht y luego obtuvo la medalla de bronce en los 10.000 metros en el Campeonato Europeo en Birmingham. En la categoría masculina de los 5 kilómetros se verá el duelo entre el francés Jimmy Gressier, campeón mundial de 10.000 metros, y el noruego Jakob Ingebrigtsen, campeón olímpico y cuatro veces campeón europeo de 5.000. Gressier, que terminó quinto en la media maratón de la última edición del Mundial de ruta de 2023, estuvo a punto de batir el récord mundial de 5 kilómetros cuando logró un récord europeo de 12:51 en Lille en abril. Solo Berihu Aregawi (12:49) y Yomif Kejelcha (12:50) han corrido más rápido que él. Ingebrigtsen, tras las finales de la Liga Diamante y el Ultimate, será su tercer fin de semana consecutivo corriendo y regresará a las calles de la ciudad donde corrió su primer, y hasta ahora único, medio maratón en 2024. Además, solo ha corrido los 5 kilómetros en ruta una vez hasta la fecha: en Stavanger en 2020, donde registró un tiempo de 13:28. La keniana Agnes Ngetich consiguió su primer título mundial con una victoria aplastante en el Mundial de cross en Tallahassee en enero, antes de marcar un tiempo de 28:58 en los 10 kilómetros en Lille, el tercer mejor tiempo de la historia. Ngetich, poseedora del récord mundial de 10 kilómetros, corrió en 1:03:04 en su debut en la media maratón en Valencia en 2024 y regresó un año después para ganar con un tiempo de 1:03:08. Estas siguen siendo la segunda y la tercera mejores marcas de la historia, solo superadas por el récord mundial de Letesenbet Gidey de 1:02:52. Su único tropiezo en el año llegó en el medio maratón de Nueva York en marzo, en el que fue decimotercera, algo a lo que se quiere agarrar la etíope Tsigie Gebreselama, que se perfila como una de las rivales más fuertes. La subcampeona mundial de cross ocupa el cuarto puesto en el 'ranking' mundial de carreras en ruta y es la participante más rápida de Copenhague este año, tras haber ganado el medio maratón de Lisboa en marzo. Su compañera de equipo etíope, Ftaw Zeray, también ha impresionado esta temporada. Ganó en París con una marca personal de 1:05:12 en marzo y, al mes siguiente, obtuvo el segundo lugar en Estambul. Zeray finalizó sexta en la media maratón del Campeonato Mundial de Atletismo en Ruta de 2023. En la categoría masculina los kenianos Nicholas Kipkorir, el más rápido de la temporada con 58:08 en Lisboa, y Daniel Ebenyo, subcampeón mundial de 10.000 metros en 2023, consiguieron medallas en la última edición del Mundial de ruta en 2023 y volverán a luchar por un puesto en el podio en la capital danesa, donde se enfrentarán a un grupo formidable de atletas, entre los que destacan otros medallistas importantes como el sueco Andreas Almgren, medallista de bronce mundial en los 10.000 metros, y el ugandés Joshua Cheptegei, múltiple campeón olímpico y mundial. El poseedor del récord italiano, Yemaneberhan Crippa, también está en acción. El atleta de 29 años terminó cuarto en los 10.000 metros europeos, ganados por Almgren, y estableció su récord nacional de 59:01 en febrero.

articles.title: Kenenisa Bekele regresa al maratón de Berlín... con 44 años
articles.standfirst: El etíope, campeón olímpico en 5.000 y 10.000, vuelve a la distancia casi un año después de que no llegara a meta en el maratón de Nueva York
articles.summary: El etíope, campeón olímpico en 5.000 y 10.000, vuelve a la distancia casi un año después de que no llegara a meta en el maratón de Nueva York
articles.body: Kenenisa Bekele regresa al maratón y lo hará en la cita de Berlín, que se disputa el próximo 27 de septiembre. Los organizadores han anunciado la incorporación de última hora del etíope a una carrera en la que no estará el gran foco actual de la distancia, el plusmarquista mundial Sabastian Sawe, por lesión. Bekele, múltiple campeón olímpico y mundial en 5.000 y 10.000 metros, ha logrado sus mejores marcas en los 42,195 kilómetros en la capital alemana, que le valieron el triunfo: 2.03:03 (2016) y 2.01:41 (2019), ambas marcas fueron en aquel momento las segundas mejores de la historia en la distancia. El último maratón completo del etíope, que también atesora 11 medallas de oro en los Mundiales de cross, fue el de los Juegos de París de 2024, en el que quedó trigésimo noveno, con 2.12:24. El pasado año no pudo terminar en Nueva York. Los organizadores del maratón alemán también han confirmado las incorporaciones de Alisa Vainio, campeona de Europa de maratón en Birmingham con récord de los campeonatos (2.22:26) y la alemana Laura Hottenrott. En el caso de Vainio, correrá su séptimo maratón en 12 meses.

articles.title: Olympic Snowboarder Chloe Kim, Former NFL RB Rashad Jennings Announced for 'The Traitors' S5 Cast
articles.summary: Chloe Kim is following up her silver medal win at the 2026 Milan Cortina Olympics with an appearance on reality TV.
articles.body:
Chloe Kim is following up her silver medal win at the 2026 Milan Cortina Olympics with an appearance on reality TV.

Kim was announced Friday as part of the cast for the new season of The Traitors , which will broadcast on NBC and Peacock.

She is one of two athletes in the cast alongside former NFL running back Rashad Jennings.

Kim, 26, won the third Olympic medal of her career with a halfpipe silver in February.

Jennings, 41, played in seven NFL seasons, including three campaigns with the New York Giants from 2014 to 2016.

This marks the second straight season in which The Traitors has featured multiple contestants connected to professional sports.

Season 4 of the show featured former Olympic figure skaters Johnny Weir and Tara Lipinski as well as Donna Kelce, the mother of Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce and Philadelphia Eagles legend Jason Kelce.

Organisers have apologised for playing the North Korean national anthem for the South Korean men's hockey team at the Asian Games in Japan.

South Korea, who thrashed Bangladesh 5-0, looked confused as the incorrect national anthem was played.

South Korea's Yonhap news agency reported that Bangladesh's national anthem followed before South Korea's actual anthem was played.

A stadium announcer did apologise for the mistake.

"This is a really serious problem. When we protested, they said, 'We're sorry. It wasn't that it wasn't prepared; there was a mistake on the part of those responsible for playing it'," South Korea coach Min Tae-seok said.

"But this is something that simply should never happen."

North Korea's national anthem, along with other symbols of the secretive state, are banned in South Korea.

The two countries are still technically at war, after the 1950-53 conflict between the two ended without a peace treaty.

The build-up to the Asian Games, which officially starts on Saturday, has already seen complaints from teams about the quality and amount of accommodation.

A member of the South Korea basketball team posted a video of a leaking pipe and soaked floor in his room, with the caption: "Please help me."

Some teams were also stranded at the airport for up to six hours when they landed this week.

Field hockey at the Asian Games started on Friday and runs until 3 October.

Latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract 📺Werro and Bol were not at the StoneX Stadium in London on Friday, so Hodgkinson cruised to victory in a time of 1:56.40 to defend her Athlos crown.Athlos is an all-women's event which was launched last year by Reddit founder Alexis Ohanian, who is the husband of 23-time tennis Grand Slam champion Serena Williams.Hodgkinson said after winning: "It's pretty sick! But I've just had to alter my approach. I've had to take my foot off the speed [training], because that's when it's most risky."

articles.title: Olympic swimmer Réka György calls out Virginia Governor Spanberger for withdrawing female sports regulation
articles.summary: Réka György, who lost an NCAA swimming final spot to Lia Thomas, slams Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger for withdrawing a female sports regulation.
articles.body: Hungarian Olympian Réka György, who lost a place in an NCAA swimming final after competing against transgender swimmer Lia Thomas, criticized Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s administration for abandoning a proposed regulation intended to protect female sports and private spaces. György was one of three female swimmers who petitioned the Virginia Board of Health to enact the regulation last year. The board unanimously approved the petition under former Gov. Glenn Youngkin, but the regulatory action was withdrawn in July after Spanberger took office. "It’s really sad for me because I had the petition filed a year ago, and Youngkin approved it and wanted to take the next step and protect female athletes and female spaces in Virginia," György told OutKick. VIRGINIA GOVERNOR ABIGAIL SPANBERGER QUIETLY ROLLS BACK YOUNGKIN'S PLANS TO PROTECT GIRLS' SPORTS "I don’t like to see that people are using their power, especially political power, to make decisions and hurt other people. And also, it’s coming from a female." György added that she was "really disappointed" by the decision. György filed the petition in April 2025 alongside former Roanoke College swimmers Lily Mullens and Carter Satterfield. It asked the Board of Health to adopt regulations preventing biological males from participating on female-only athletic teams or entering female-designated spaces where women and girls could be undressing. After receiving more than 2,300 public comments, the board voted 14–0 in August 2025 to begin the regulatory process. The Youngkin administration subsequently approved a Notice of Intended Regulatory Action, which was published that November. SUPREME COURT MAKES RULING ON TRANS ATHLETES IN WOMEN'S SPORTS However, the Spanberger administration withdrew the action on July 30, after an additional public-comment period had concluded. The withdrawal was not accompanied by an announcement from the governor’s office and was later published in the Virginia Register of Regulations. The official notice said the State Board of Health would not proceed "upon review of statutory authority." György questioned why the administration did not call greater public attention to the decision. "I have a feeling that she’s afraid of the backlash of people, what they’re going to say or think," György said. "Other than that, I don’t know what her motivation is." György’s advocacy stems from her experience at the 2022 NCAA Division I Women’s Swimming and Diving Championships. The Virginia Tech swimmer finished 17th in the preliminary round of the 500-yard freestyle, one place short of advancing to the consolation final. Thomas, a biological male who identifies as a transgender woman, qualified for the championship final and went on to win the national title. "Because the rule-makers let him compete in the women’s category, I got bumped out from the final," György said. "I got 17th, and I wasn’t allowed to swim in the finals. It ended up being me who got knocked out of the finals at night." THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! György represented Hungary at the 2016 Rio Olympics and was a two-time ACC champion and two-time NCAA All-American during her career at Virginia Tech. She said she had devoted approximately 18 years to swimming before her final collegiate championship appearance. "I put everything into swimming that I had," she said. "The 2022 NCAA Championships was my senior year in college, so I was ready to retire from swimming, but before I did that, give my best. I had everything that I was capable of putting into practices to prepare myself to give my best at that competition. "And the chance to actually swim in the final was taken away." György also recalled sharing a women’s locker room with Thomas during the championship meet. "You were in just constant fear," she said. "You had no idea when he was going to enter the locker room." György explained that putting on a high-level racing suit can take between 15 and 25 minutes, preventing swimmers from simply changing quickly and leaving. "I was always looking behind my shoulder because I had no idea when my privacy was going to be robbed away," she said. "You try to cover yourself, which usually you don’t do because you are surrounded by other females and you don’t have that issue. But that competition was different." The experience ultimately prompted György to become an outspoken advocate for sex-separated athletic competition and private spaces. "I just had this feeling that I had to speak up because, obviously, the people who were in charge of that competition didn’t do anything to protect us females," she said. "One day, maybe I will have a daughter, and I don’t want my daughter to be in a situation where I had to share the locker room and compete against a male." György, who continues to live in Virginia, joined the petition effort after being contacted about the controversy involving Mullens, Satterfield and the Roanoke College women’s swimming team. In 2023, members of the team objected when a transgender student sought to join the women’s roster. Roanoke College later said the student had chosen not to compete. György said she has not yet contacted Spanberger because she only recently learned the regulatory action had been withdrawn, but she plans to seek a conversation with the governor. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I want to tell her that I hope she sees where I’m coming from," György said. "I hope she sees where other people are coming from when we are trying to protect little girls and females in sports and women-only spaces." "Title IX was created for a reason," she added. "I really do hope that she is going to follow this rule, and she is going to stand up for women in Virginia."

articles.title: Athlos London: Keely Hodgkinson powers to victory in speed suit at all-female event
articles.summary: Keely Hodgkinson powers to victory in a full-body speed suit before being presented with a Tiffany & Co crown as Athlos makes its London debut.
articles.body:
Keely Hodgkinson powered to victory in a custom-made full-body speed suit before being presented with a Tiffany & Co crown as Athlos made its London debut.

Hodgkinson was greeted by loud cheers as she emerged on to a stage and revealed the all-black aerodynamic outfit at the third staging of the all-female athletics meet.

The 24-year-old ensured she ended a mixed year with a dominant 800m victory in front of a sellout home crowd at StoneX Stadium, bursting clear on the back straight and crossing the line in one minute 56.40 seconds.

Speaking about the outfit, Hodgkinson told BBC Sport: "This has been like a year in the making. It's a mixture of fashion and speed and science all coming together for maybe the future of athletics.

"It was a real honour for them to choose me to put this out first. We weren't sure when we were going to wear it.

"But an all-women's event that's all about the glitz and the glamour and putting eyes on women, a bit of a moment, I think was the perfect way to finish the season."

Created by Alexis Ohanian, Reddit co-founder and husband of tennis' 23-time Grand Slam singles champion Serena Williams, Athlos was staging a meet for the first time outside of New York.

In addition to the silver Tiffany crown awarded to winners instead of medals, a top prize of $65,000 (£48,500) was on offer in each event.

The single-night meet included seven disciplines, each featuring six athletes, with money on offer for each position from a total event prize pot of $1.05m (£790,500).

American sprint stars Gabby Thomas and Sha'Carri Richardson were among the champions amid a party atmosphere which featured a live track-side DJ.

Hodgkinson ends mixed year with crown and a smile

The athletes had arrived on a red carpet in north London but Hodgkinson saved her starring moment for the main event.

The eye-catching speed suit, reminiscent of that worn by Cathy Freeman in winning Olympic 400m gold in 2000, featured an open back and a hood with a ponytail opening - the latter, she said, was non-negotiable - while colour-changing 3D-printed nodes reduced drag in key areas.

Paired with dark sunglasses and Nike's latest carbon-plated spikes, it helped Hodgkinson achieve her first victory since the London Diamond League in July.

It has been a year of record-breaking highs and frustrating setbacks for the Olympic champion.

An indoor season in which she landed her first world 800m title and smashed a 24-year world record heightened expectations that she would take down the sport's longest-standing mark outdoors.

But a nasty fall suffered on a post-session cool down run in July, and a recurrence of the hamstring injury which kept her out of action for much of 2025 at the European Championships, conspired to hinder her progress.

While still improving her British record this summer, Hodgkinson finished second to breakout Swiss star Audrey Werro at both the European Championships and inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship.

However, with Swiss athlete Valentina Rosamilia finishing more than two seconds behind, she ended the season with a smile on her face and a crown on her head as she danced on stage with the night's other winners.

Training partner Georgia Hunter Bell was pipped to victory in the mile by Poland's Klaudia Kazimierska.

Diamond League champion Kazimierska, who denied Hunter Bell in her bid to win a fourth major title of 2026 at last week's World Athletics Ultimate Championship, squeezed past on the inside to edge the Briton in four minutes 19.43 seconds.

That close finish left Ohanian in disbelief as he watched trackside alongside tennis great Williams and their children, with famous athletes and celebrities also present.

Former world champion Richardson stormed to victory in the 100m in 10.80 seconds, as Britons Imani-Lara Lansiquot (11.35) and Daryll Neita (11.36) placed fourth and fifth respectively.

Olympic 200m champion Thomas took victory in the final race of the night, winning the 200m in 22.13 seconds, while Dominican Olympic champion Marileidy Paulino overhauled Norway's Henriette Jaeger to win the 400m in 48.73 seconds.

There were also wins for Americans Alaysha Johnson in the 100m hurdles and Alyssa Jones in the long jump.

Ohanian has been clear about his eventual intention to make Athlos a global season-long league.

Athlos was supposed to expand to a two-day event in 2026, but the New York meeting scheduled for 2 October was cancelled following consultation with the athletes at the end of a long season.

Instead, Ohanian now hopes to align Athlos within the global athletics calendar from next year.

How that will work remains to be seen. The Diamond League, athletics' premier season-long series, runs from May until September, while the introduction of the Ultimate Championship - joining the Olympics and the World Championships on the calendar - means every season will now feature a global competition of some description.

American Masai Russell, who broke the 100m hurdles world record last month, was among the late Athlos withdrawals following last week's Ultimate, organised by the sport's governing body and offering record prize pot of $10m.

'Built differently' - Hodgkinson reveals hamstring abnormality

World Road Running Championships 2026 - watch across the BBC

After a week in which countless female athletes denounced a controversial sports betting company advertisement featuring actress Sydney Sweeney, Ohanian said he wanted Friday's event to put the attention back on the "actual athletes".

It achieved just that, with some of the world's top female athletes going head-to-head in competitive events while also being allowed the space to express their personalities.

Ohanian is determined to bridge a perceived disconnect between the attention on the sport at each Olympic Games compared to the rest of the calendar in those four-year cycles.

The 43-year-old set up the Angel City FC women's football club in Los Angeles six years ago after leaving Reddit, and purchased a 10% stake in Women's Super League team Chelsea in 2025.

At Athlos, the athletes who have competed in its early events were offered equity in the league, the idea being that they will be rewarded if it is successful.

"I would have loved to have had this when I was younger. Hopefully the youngsters can see this and have their time one day," Hodgkinson said.

While some have criticised the exclusion of men's events, Ohanian said an initial focus on female athletes was a business decision and he has identified the 2028 edition, around the Los Angeles Olympics, an opportunity to expand in that regard.

Athlos set out to be different, and it definitely felt that. There was as much showbusiness as there was sport - this was all about the "event".

Athletes arrived on bespoke London buses and walked the red carpet before their event. Several of the athletes said they enjoyed having the spotlight on them and being able to combine their sport with fashion and many will now be part of London Fashion Week.

Georgia Hunter Bell emerged from a melee of screaming children telling her she was their idol onto the red carpet and said she felt "valued".

It was certainly noisy, and the resident DJ meant at times it felt more like you were in a club than an athletics meet. But the athletes and fans seemed to buy into the vibe.

One man told me he had been to 27 world championships and five Olympics and wasn't sure he'd enjoy Athlos, but loved it. A woman whose daughter is part of the athletics club who train at StoneX Stadium said she thought it was "remarkable" and "inspirational".

There will be learnings from this first trip to London, but as a starting point, it felt like it lived up to its hype.

articles.title: Trump says son paid back Putin ally for 'totally allowed' wedding festivities gift
articles.summary: Daughter in-law Bettina Trump confirms that Umar Kremlev partially funded two nights of their three-day festivities on a private island in the Bahamas.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has said his son paid back a Russian oligarch with close ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin for hosting post-wedding festivities in the Bahamas.

Asked in the Oval Office about Umar Kremlev's involvement in Donald Trump Jr's celebrations, Trump said it is "totally allowed" and that it is "very common" to give wedding parties for others.

After an investigation said Kremlev paid "hundreds of thousands of dollars", the couple confirmed he partially funded two nights of their three-day festivities on a private island as a gift.

Trump did not say how he knew the Putin ally was paid back. The BBC has not verified payment was made and has contacted Trump Jr.

Trump Jr, the president's eldest son, is a private citizen, so it is not illegal for him to accept gifts from a foreign national.

But ethics watchdog groups have said that the president's son accepting an expensive gift from someone associated with a foreign head of state presents the appearance of a conflict of interest – even if Trump Jr is not a US government employee.

President Trump's ties to Russia have raised questions since his 2016 campaign, and led to a special counsel investigation into a meeting attended by Trump Jr with a Russian operative at Trump Tower.

Donald Trump Jr and Bettina Trump say Putin ally paid for some wedding festivities as a 'gift'

Kremlev runs the International Boxing Association (IBA), which is funded by the state-backed Gazprom energy company. The organisation was suspended by the Olympic Committee in part over its failure to report its ties to the Russian energy giant.

Kremlev was also a member of a delegation that visited China with Putin in May. He has been given the Order of Friendship, a top state honour, by the Russian president, according to ProPublica, which published the investigation about the wedding events.

Trump Jr's spokesperson told the news outlet that the president's son and Kremlev were personal friends and did not have "a business relationship".

Kremlev's office told ProPublica that he and Trump Jr met a few years ago and "have a friendly relationship".

The BBC has contacted representatives for Kremlev for comment.

articles.title: 'We don’t want to leave a white elephant': OCA defends decision to do away with traditional Games village
articles.summary: Asian Games 2026 News: NAGOYA: The Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) on Friday defended the Asian Games organisers’ decision to do away with a traditional Games village and acco.
articles.body: NAGOYA: The Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) on Friday defended the Asian Games organisers’ decision to do away with a traditional Games village and accommodate athletes across containers, hotels and cruise ships.The decision to scrap plans for an athletes’ village came after the Games budget more than tripled from the original estimate of 80-100 billion yen (Rs 48.6cr-61cr).OCA director general Husain Al-Musallam said that while an athletes’ village was desirable, its utility after the Games often did not justify the cost of construction.“You spend so much money building the athletes’ village and then we need to see what’s the utilisation of it after the Games. Considering the cost and size of the Games, we need to be a little bit flexible. The athletes’ village is good to look at. But at the end of the day, we need to be practical,” he said at a press conference here on Friday.Tayyab Ikram, head of the OCA coordination commission for the Games, said the decision was driven by the high cost of real estate and the desire to avoid leaving behind a “white elephant” after the Games.“We had clear statistics about what is happening in the real estate values. We don’t want to leave a white elephant after the Games here. It was not easy to discuss, but it was also not a compromise because we found a very unique kind of alternative,” he said.The tradition of an athletes’ village began at the 1982 Asian Games in New Delhi. The hosts of the next two editions — Doha and Riyadh — will have such villages, but Ikram, who is also FIH president, stressed that it was not mandatory for organisers to provide one.TWO-YEAR WAIT FOR BIDIndia’s bid to host the 2038 Asian Games will have to wait until 2028 for a decision on the host nation. India is among six countries to have expressed interest in hosting the Games.“We have received interest from India, Philippines and four other countries to host the Asian Games in 2038. This shows the popularity of the Asian Games,” Al-Musallam said.He said the OCA executive board had already approved the broad evaluation process.“There are 12 more years to go. The calendar is well-established. The executive board has taken a decision to create an evaluation committee to visit all those countries next year and then submit an initial report.“Based on that report, we will have a shortlist and then go for another visit 9-10 years before the Games and submit the final report,” he said.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Olympic Council of Asia president says politics have already entered into the Asian Games
articles.summary: The president of the Olympic Council of Asia acknowledged Saturday that politics — in the form of a welcoming ceremony involving Taiwan — had already entered...
articles.body:
NAGOYA, Japan (AP) — The president of the Olympic Council of Asia acknowledged Saturday that politics — in the form of a welcoming ceremony involving Taiwan — had already entered into the Asian Games .

He did not sound pleased about it, speaking just hours before the official opening ceremony on Saturday.

Some event at the Asian Games began several days ago to accommodate a packed schedule and more than 17,000 athletes and officials. Up to 5,000 are housed on a cruise ship .

"I don't think, you know, the politicians or politics should be involved in sports," said Sheikh Joaan bin Hamad Al Thani, speaking with media at the Asian Games.

He is the younger brother of the Emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim bin Al Thani.

Sheikh Joaan was asked about an incident Friday at the Asian Games in which Taiwan's sports minister, Lee Yang, was temporarily barred from a welcoming ceremony and a flag-raising.

Lee was later allowed to participate and the OCA attributed the incident to a misunderstanding.

"We don't mix sports with politics and we already have," Sheikh Joaan said. "We're going to take — if something like this will happen, we have our way of taking care of it. And all the delegations know what the protocol is and what should be done, and what shouldn't be done."

Lee is a two-time Olympic gold medalist in badminton. He won gold twice in doubles — 2020 and 2024 — each time defeating a Chinese pair in the final.

Taiwan competes in the Asian Games and the Olympics under the name of Chinese Taipei and without its flag due to China's claim on the island off its east coast.

Taiwan media reported the OCA had issued an order barring Lee. Taiwan media reported that Taiwan officials asked to see the order but officials were unable to produce it.

"We chose to stick to our principles," Chen Shih-kwei, a vice president of the Chinese Taipei Olympic Committee, said.

"We asked the local organizing committee and the OCA to uphold the Olympic spirit, so that we could attend all events equally and with dignity," Chen added. "We insisted on this, and then negotiations began. We stood firm on our dignity and principles."

Lee later told Taiwanese reporters that "we are doing our best to safeguard our rights and do not want to be subjected to any form of suppression."

"We also hope more Taiwanese athletes can perform at their best and give their all at the games so that Taiwan can be more visible on the international stage."

articles.title: El supersónico traje que quiere revolucionar el atletismo: "Hay tanta ciencia detrás que no te lo creerías"
articles.standfirst: Keely Hodgkinson, campeona olímpica, usa un uniforme que mezcla moda, velocidad y ciencia para ganar los 800 metros de Athlos
articles.summary: Keely Hodgkinson, campeona olímpica, usa un uniforme que mezcla moda, velocidad y ciencia para ganar los 800 metros de Athlos
articles.body: "Es un proyecto que ha tardado casi un año en gestarse. Es una mezcla de moda, velocidad y ciencia que se unen para lo que quizás sea el futuro del atletismo". Fueron las palabras de Keely Hodgkinson, la vigente campeona olímpica de 800 metros, tras su victoria en Athlos, una competición de atletismo profesional y exclusiva para mujeres, que se celebró en Londres, en el que deporte y espectáculo van de la mano (contó con un DJ en vivo a pie de pista). Hodgkinson apareció en la pista enfundada en un traje negro, que recordaba al que portó Cathy Freeman en los Juegos Olímpicos de Sídney 2000. Un cuarto de siglo después la evolución del material ha llevado a este uniforme a un nuevo nivel. "Fue genial poder inspirarme en el pasado y, al mismo tiempo, hacerlo mío", comentó Hodgkinson al ser preguntada por Freeman. Creado por Nike, el mono es una versión mejorada y, según palabras de la plusmarquista mundial de los 800 metros en pista cubierta, ajustada a las normas de World Athletics y con mejor tecnología. Carece de cierres y cuenta con las mínimas costuras posibles. Los componentes aerodinámicos se han colocado a lo largo del traje para ayudar a reducir la resistencia al aire. El traje se desarrolló en el túnel de viento y luego en pista, con una rodilla articulada, un refuerzo de movilidad 4D y aberturas alrededor de la espalda y las axilas diseñadas para permitir la libertad de movimiento y la termorregulación. "El material... Han aprendido muchísimo sobre cómo hacer que la piel sea más rápida, que los humanos sean más rápidos... Hay tanta ciencia detrás que no te lo creerías. No estábamos seguros de cuándo lo íbamos a usar, pero en retrospectiva, un evento exclusivamente femenino, que se trata de brillo y glamour y de atraer la atención hacia las mujeres, fue perfecto", apuntó Hodgkinson que reconoció que lo había probado en Sudáfrica, con 37 grados. "Quería estar cómoda, pero también quería sentirme un poco sexy. La espalda está abierta y eso hace que sea realmente especial. Y no tengo nada de calor. Literalmente siento como si no llevara nada, para ser sincera", apostilló. Hodgkinson entró en meta con un tiempo de 1:56.40, muy lejos de su mejor marca personal (1:54.33). Como luego reconoció quizá podría haber ganado más aerodinámica si hubiera escondido su pelo dentro de la capucha del traje: "Con la resistencia del aire vas más lento con el pelo suelto, pero eso es innegociable'”. Por ese motivo, el traje incorporó a petición suya una abertura para su coleta y ranuras en la capucha diseñadas para sus gafas de sol. "No os podéis imaginar las ideas que tiene esta gente. Es una locura", finalizó la atleta británica. El triunfo le reportó, no sólo la corona de plata de Tiffany que se entregaba a los ganadores en lugar de medallas, sin un premio en metálico de 56.500 euros.

articles.title: Agathe Guillemot y Robert Farken, campeones del mundo de la milla
articles.standfirst: Se imponen a los favoritos, la etíope Freweyni Hailu y el estadounidense Yared Nuguse, que acabaron segundos
articles.summary: Se imponen a los favoritos, la etíope Freweyni Hailu y el estadounidense Yared Nuguse, que acabaron segundos
articles.body: La francesa Agathe Guillemot, con un tiempo de 4:22.74, y el alemán Robert Farken, con 3:51.80, se proclamaron campeones del mundo de la milla en Copenhague (Dinamarca). Tras el éxito de la primera edición en Riga (Letonia) en 2023, Copenhague fue designada sede para la segunda edición de los Mundiales en ruta para concluir la temporada oficial de campeonatos organizados por World Athletics. La prueba que abrió este Mundiales fue la milla, en la que Guillemot, de 27 años, sorprendió en el recorrido de 1.609 metros a la gran favorita, la etíope Freweyni Hailu, la doble campeona mundial de pista cubierta de 1.500 que repitió el segundo puesto de hace tres años en Riga. Tras dominar la primera parte de carrera, Guillemot tomó la delantera pasado el ecuador de recorrido y consiguió imprimir un ritmo que hizo sufrir a Hailu. La francesa entró en meta con un crono de 4:22.74, récord de Europa de la distancia, mientras que la etíope registró 4:24.35. Tercera fue la keniana Miriam Cherop con 4:25.71. En la categoría masculina también hubo sorpresa porque el principal favorito, el estadounidense Yared Nuguse, finalizó segundo. El medallista de bronce olímpico en 1500 metros y antiguo poseedor del récord mundial de la milla en pista cubierta llegó a Copenhague tras demostrar este mismo año su habilidad en ruta, al ganar el título estadounidense en abril con un tiempo de 3:54.06. En la capital danesa, tras liderar la prueba durante gran parte del recorrido, se quedó sin fuerza en las piernas cuando en el tramo final Robert Farken hizo un cambio de ritmo al que no supo responder. El alemán entró en meta en un tiempo de 3:51.80, aventajando en solo 53 centésimas a Nuguse (3:52.33). Tercero fue el luxemburgués Ruben Querinjean con 3:52.77, récord nacional. El español Martín Segurola, campeón de España de 3.000 metros en pista cubierta y medallista de bronce por equipos con España en el Europeo de campo a través de Lagoa, finalizó decimoquinto con 3:56.92, marca personal.

articles.title: ‘All my best wishes’: Neeraj Chopra backs Team India as Asian Games 2026 get underway
articles.summary: Asian Games 2026 News: NEW DELHI: Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra on Saturday sent his best wishes to the Indian contingent as the 20th Asian Games officially got underway in.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra on Saturday sent his best wishes to the Indian contingent as the 20th Asian Games officially got underway in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, expressing confidence that the athletes would make the country proud.Chopra, who will miss the continental showpiece after an ankle ligament injury ended his 2026 season, took to X to send his message to the Indian athletes as the Games began with a colourful opening ceremony.“All my best wishes to Team India at the Asian Games 2026! I’m sure they will all make us proud.”The Asian Games are being held from September 19 to October 4, with India competing across multiple disciplines and looking to build on its record medal haul from the previous edition.Chopra misses Games but backs Indian contingentTwo-time Asian Games gold medallist Chopra won javelin gold at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics and followed it with silver at the Paris 2024 Olympics. His absence is a significant one for India's athletics campaign after the 28-year-old suffered an ankle ligament injury during a training session.While Chopra will not be able to defend his Asian Games title, his message came as the Indian contingent began its campaign at Aichi-Nagoya.Olympic medallist Manu Bhaker and kabaddi star Pawan Sehrawat led the Indian contingent at Saturday's opening ceremony. Bhaker, a double bronze medallist at the Paris Olympics, will compete in the women's 10m air pistol, women's 25m pistol and 10m air pistol mixed team events.Ahead of the ceremony, Bhaker also reflected on being chosen as a flag bearer.“Honestly, when I found out yesterday, I had all these flashback memories of my earlier days. And, you know, when I started, I never thought that this was where I could reach one day in my sport. So, it is definitely a very heartwarming feeling. I feel really proud, really honoured, and really, really happy to be chosen as the flag bearer for my country. I just want to say thank you to God and thank you to everyone for all the love and support,” she said.ALSO READ: How India’s Asian Games medal story has changed over two decadesIndia looks to build on record Asian Games campaignThe opening ceremony at the Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium formally marked the start of the Games, with Japan's Emperor Naruhito declaring the event open.The athletes' parade featured contingents from 45 nations and the OCA Refugee Team. Sehrawat replaced shot-putter Tajinderpal Singh Toor as India's flag bearer after Toor did not receive his ceremonial kit in time.India is looking to improve on its best-ever Asian Games performance at Hangzhou in 2023, where it won 106 medals, including 28 gold, 38 silver and 40 bronze.Some competitions had already begun before the opening ceremony. India's women's cricket team reached the semifinals after defeating hosts Japan by eight wickets, while Quimcy D'Souza remained in contention for a teqball bronze after losing her women's singles semifinal.The Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games will feature around 11,000 athletes competing across 43 sports for 469 gold medals, with the closing ceremony scheduled for October 4.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.standfirst: Corre en 14:59 y pulveriza la anterior plusmarca de Marta Domínguez (15.11 en 2002) en una carrera que coronó a la etíope Likina Amebaw como campeona mundial
articles.summary: Corre en 14:59 y pulveriza la anterior plusmarca de Marta Domínguez (15.11 en 2002) en una carrera que coronó a la etíope Likina Amebaw como campeona mundial
articles.body: Marta García, subcampeona de Europa de 5.000 metros en pista, finalizó sexta, con un tiempo de 14:59, nuevo récord nacional de la distancia, los 5 kilómetros de los Mundiales de ruta de Copenhague (Dinamarca), en los que se impuso la favorita, la etíope Likina Amebaw (14:41). Marta García hizo su debut con España en una prueba de ruta en Copenhague. Su reciente plata europea en Birmingham y las posteriores competiciones en los Juegos Mediterráneos de Taranto (Italia) en 1.500 y en el Ultimate Champioship de Budapest donde logró la mejor marca española del año en 5.000 (14:43.94), la segunda mejor de su vida, la permitieron llegar a Copenhague en un excelente momento de forma. En las calles de la capital danesa, la palentina refrendó ese buen momento que atraviesa con un crono de 14:59, mejorando los 15:11 de Marta Domínguez el 1 de septiembre de 2002 en Londres. El triunfo fue par Likina Amebaw, que llegó a la cita como número uno del ránking mundial y no defraudó. Con una marca personal de 14:23 en 5 kilómetros establecida en Barcelona y 29:29 en Valencia en 10k, la etíope ganó de forma contundente con 14:41, siete segundos menos que la keniana Caroline Makandi Gitonga (14:48). Cerró el podio la australiana Rose Davies con 14:50.

articles.title: World Road Running: Ingebrigtsen pipped to 5km road title in Copenhagen
articles.summary: Jakob Ingebrigtsen is pipped to victory in the men's 5km in a thrilling finish at the World Road Running Championships in Copenhagen.
articles.body:
Jakob Ingebrigtsen was pipped to victory in the men's 5km in a thrilling finish at the World Road Running Championships in Copenhagen.

African 5,000m champion Dawit Seare found a reserve of energy to pip the Norwegian great and take gold for Eritrea, with compatriot Saymon Amanuel winning bronze.

Ingebrigtsen, 26, was taking part in only his sixth race of an injury-hit season, eight days after he won the 5,000m on the track at the Ultimate Athletics Championships in Budapest.

The Olympic 5,000m champion looked well out of contention until about the final kilometre but powered through to lead, until Seare caught and passed him in the dying stages to win in 12 minutes and 56 seconds.

Likina Amebaw of Ethiopia dominated the women's 5km, just six days after winning $150,000 (£112,000) for victory in the 5,000m in Budapest.

Amebaw was imperious, making an early break to win in decisive fashion in 14:41.

Caroline Gitonga of Kenya was seven seconds behind in second place and Rose Davies of Australia won bronze as Britain's Hannah Nuttall (15:08) came home in 10th.

Robert Farken of Germany was a surprise winner of the men's mile.

American Yared Nuguse led from the gun but was caught in the final 100m as Farken won in 3:51.80 for his first major title.

Jake Heyward of Britain was 11th in a personal best on the roads of 3:55.76.

Agathe Guillemot of France won the women's mile in 4:22.74, the fastest time in the world this year on the road, after timing her attack to perfection to beat Freweyni Hailu of Ethiopia.

Kenyan Mirriam Cherop was third with Katie Snowden of Great Britain 16th.

The half-marathon titles will be decided on Sunday, with the elite races forming part of a two-day festival of running in the Danish capital.

articles.title: Ole Miss hosts LSU in top game in the country, but Rebels not even most decorated football team on own campus
articles.summary: The Ole Miss Special Olympics flag football club won gold in Minneapolis, and now these mini celebrities are cheering on the Rebels against LSU.
articles.body: While Oxford, Mississippi is the epicenter of the college football world this weekend, with Ole Miss set to host its former head coach Lane Kiffin and LSU on Saturday night, the town is also home to a defending national champion in football. Flag football, that is. The Ole Miss Special Olympics College Flag Football Club represented the state of Mississippi over the summer at the Special Olympics in Minneapolis and, well, "Hotty Toddy," the Rebels won the whole darn thing. Gold medal and all. Pretty sure that makes this group of football Rebels the most decorated on campus. "Hopefully, they (the football team) see us and they’re like, ‘Well, we’ve got to go get a national championship now," Ole Miss senior Jason Skocy said with a smile. FROM FOOTBALL SATURDAYS TO ROUTINE WEEKDAYS, THE MUSIC NEVER STOPS AT THIS UT HOUSE FULL OF COLLEGE MUSICIANS EVEN ON OPENING WEEKEND, FOOTBALL PLAYERS AT CLEMSON, LSU MIGHT BE UPSTAGED ON CAMPUS BY THESE FURRY FRIENDS Skocy is a center for the flag football team, which is comprised of Ole Miss students like Skocy, who are called partners, along with local and regional individuals with intellectual disabilities. They are called athletes. Flag football in this category is played 5-on-5, and for each team, there are always 3 athletes to 2 partners on the field at all times. Make no mistake, there might be flags instead of tackles, but this is still football. There are playbooks, touchdowns, running, passing and players chasing each other all over the field. "These kids have play cards on their arms, I call plays," said Hunter Crabbs, the intramural sports and sports clubs coordinator at Ole Miss who was one of the coaches of the gold medal flag team. "It’s a much smaller playbook than what we might be using on Saturday night (against LSU), but it’s a very similar process." Abbreviated or not, something in the playbook is working. After earning the right to represent the state of Mississippi at the Special Olympics by defeating a team from Mississippi State, the Rebels overcame all kinds of adversity in Minnesota to bring Mississippi its first-ever intercollegiate gold medal in flag football. They lost their first two games in Minneapolis, felt down in the dumps, but rallied to get to the championship game. In that final game, against Iowa, one of the teams to tag an early loss on the Rebels in pool play, one key player for Ole Miss went down with a serious injury. The score was tight at the time. But the Rebels dug deep again, and came away with the emotional victory. Chants of "Hotty Toddy" rang through the Ole Miss fan section and along the Ole Miss sideline. "We were so excited, we were all jumping around," said 27-year-old Madison Dennis, an athlete who plays defense for the team. She is also the only woman on the team. "We honestly couldn’t believe it. It was awesome to bring home gold back to Ole Miss." The Rebels brought back so much more than gold. They brought back memories, and friendships, and confidence and self-esteem that had grown and blossomed. "There’s a couple of our athletes who, going into this trip, I would have said they’re probably going to be maybe a little shy, maybe not want to interact with other teams," Skocy said. "I was completely wrong. They were out there, making friends, staying up, playing Xbox in the lobby. It was cool to see." The team also took a trip to Mall of America, toured Minneapolis and went to a baseball game. There were also all kinds of fun activities in the athletes’ Olympic Village that kept the players busy. For Dennis, making friends became just as important as chasing down quarterbacks, which she does with glee. "Oh yes, I did that," Dennis smiled as she recalled her pursuits of opposing quarterbacks. "I just love flag football. And it has helped me build new friendships, different people that I would have never gotten to meet. "And the partners, I like having them there to help us. That’s a pretty cool thing." articles.body: Simone Biles has spent years making history on the gymnastics floor. But in May 2026, the Olympic champion offered fans a glimpse of a different kind of investment, one involving luxury fashion and her life beyond competition. With a playful Instagram Story featuring Christian Louboutin heels, Biles showed that building a business portfolio can also leave room for personal style and a little indulgence.Simone Biles' Christian Louboutin heels bring a luxury twist to her business journeyThe 29-year-old gymnast shared the photo on Instagram Stories on Wednesday, May 27, giving followers a close-up of her white Christian Louboutin Hot Chick pumps. The shoes, known for their signature red soles and elegant design, typically retail for around $945 to $1,045 in the United States.Biles added a caption that quickly caught attention:“The goal this year was to invest in nice \[expletive\] shoes, for work of course 🤍”The remark offered a fun look at her mindset in 2026. While Biles has made major moves in business, her latest purchase was not another sports venture or corporate deal. It was a luxury fashion choice that she jokingly framed as a work-related investment.That small detail made the post feel relatable. Even someone with an extraordinary list of achievements can enjoy setting personal goals, treating herself and finding confidence in what she wears.The shoes also fit a broader shift in Biles' life. Her identity now reaches well beyond gymnastics, with business, public appearances and personal style becoming part of her story. The Instagram post did not announce a new venture, but it showed a lighter side of the work that comes with building a life after years of elite competition.Simone Biles expands her business portfolio with Taste of GoldBiles' shoe post came just months after she entered a new business space. On March 25, 2026, she opened Taste of Gold, a restaurant at George Bush Intercontinental Airport in Houston, Texas.The restaurant draws inspiration from her Olympic career, blending food with details that celebrate her achievements. Its décor includes a photo from her medal-winning balance beam performance, while the menu features sandwiches, Tex-Mex dishes and a signature item called “Simone Skewers.”Taste of Gold marks a notable step for Biles, giving her a business presence outside the world of sports and endorsements. It also shows how athletes can turn their names and personal stories into ventures that connect with fans in new ways.Still, her latest fashion purchase offered a more personal glimpse into that evolution. Biles has not suggested that the Louboutin heels are tied to a specific business deal. Her caption instead mixed humour with the idea of dressing for work, leaving room for the simple pleasure of buying something she loves.Biles' achievements remain remarkable. She has earned 11 Olympic medals and 30 World Championship medals, placing her among the most decorated gymnasts in history. Her husband, Chicago Bears safety Jonathan Owens, has also supported her career, including travelling to major competitions.As Biles continues to explore life beyond the gym, her ventures may range from restaurants to other business opportunities. articles.title: Asian Games debut beckons for Deepu Mallesh after years of crowdfunded climbing
articles.summary: Asian Games 2026 News: CHENNAI: For speed climber Deepu Mallesh, getting to the starting line has sometimes been as difficult as getting to the top of the climbing wall. Fro.
articles.body: CHENNAI: For speed climber Deepu Mallesh, getting to the starting line has sometimes been as difficult as getting to the top of the climbing wall. From 2019-24, the 28-year-old relied on crowdfunding for most of his competitions. But financial constraints never stopped the Karnataka lad from pushing forward.He repeatedly lowered his own national record, with his latest mark coming at the Asian Championships earlier this year, where he clocked 5.39 seconds. The next stop in his journey is Japan, where he will make his maiden Asian Games appearance.“Competing in the Asian Games will help me on the path to Olympic qualification. Last year, the entire preparation was focused on making it to the Asian Games. I want to go below my national record and be a good competitor to others without putting pressure on me,” Deepu, who is also an online instructor, told TOI.While Deepu’s parents wanted him to study, he chose climbing as an escape route and tried the sport following his coach Shiva’s recommendation. The sport being included in the Olympics back then was a major push for Deepu to stay on.“Most of my competitions were crowdfunded with the help of my climbing community and others. The 2023 season was very difficult. To qualify for the Paris Olympics, I had to compete in six World Cups to improve my rankings and at least get to compete in Olympic qualifiers. But I could only participate in three WCs due to fund shortage and visa issues. Crowdfunding is always very risky. Until the very end, you will not know how much money you are going to get, how much you are going to spend, how much you have to work with. I could not plan things properly, but somehow, I tried to manage with whatever I had,” Deepu, who lowered the NR from 6.22s to 5.39s over the last few years, added.Just as the 2023 season was important for Deepu, next year will be equally crucial, with him having to compete in all the WCs and earn ranking points.
